newsitem.title: UK: Brazil seen compensating coffee creditors -sources.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen compensating coffee creditors -sources.

text.p: A European court has ruled Brazil must compensate companies for losses incurred in the so-called Operation London Terminal, masterminded in 1986 to boost sagging world prices, sources close to the proceedings said.
"They (the Brazilian government) have to settle their old debts, which are extremely high," said a London-based source close to the proceedings.
The 1986 deal is also known in the trade as Operation Patricia after the daughter of the head of the now defunct Brazilian Coffee Institute (IBC) who masterminded it.
It involved the buying of futures contracts involving some 600,000 60-kg bags of coffee - or 36,000 tonnes - from London's terminal market by some 18 companies.

The operation, a closely guarded secret, aimed to return some of the terminal coffee into Brazil for domestic consumption with the remainder re-sold once prices spiked higher, said sources familiar with the operation.
The Brazilian government also planned to use the coffee to build strategic stockpiles around Europe.
But the operation failed to lift prices and some participants and creditors were left holding hefty debts and much of the coffee lost.
But after years of legal wrangling, an Italian court in Trieste in July ruled the Brazilian government must compensate the creditors who lost money in the operation.
The Brazilian government, however, has contested the ruling and a new hearing is set for November 19, said the sources.
A senior Brazilian commodities official this week said he knew nothing of the Italian court ruling.

But the four companies, possibly five, likely to be compensated are set to receive some 338,739 60-kg bags of coffee - stored in a Trieste warehouse - for the money lost during the operation, the sources said.
"This old coffee might be a small piece of sugar in the face of a very big and bitter wrangle. It is a small gift but it will never compensate the big credit the exporters lost," said one source.
One of the creditors alone is said to be owed at least $150 million, he added.

While the companies involved in the scheme to take delivery of coffee from the futures market, had been promised in 1986 that they would be compensated later in cash or coffee, the Brazilian government has only doled out $15 million, and guarantees of the coffee stored in Trieste.
But 10 years on, the compensation expected to be received by some of the trade houses involved was said to be small, especially since they would have to pay for the warehousing costs in Trieste.
"They are getting the coffee but as soon as they get it they must pay cash for all the warehousing costs," said the source.
